s: Russia (a transcontinental country in Eastern Europe and North Asia)

russisch.et: From Middle High German rūzesch, from Rūz, from Old High German Rūzo, from Medieval Latin Russus, from Medieval Greek Ῥῶς (Rhôs). By surface analysis, Russe + -isch.

s: proboscis; trunk (prolonged nose of certain mammals, notably elephants)
proboscis (similar organ in certain insects, etc.)
beak (human nose, especially a large one)
Rüssel.et:
With irregular shortening of the stem vowel from Middle High German rüeȥel, from Old High German *ruoȥil, from Proto-West Germanic *wrōtil.
Compare typologically Polish ryj, Russian ры́ло (rýlo) (akin to рыть (rytʹ)).

Ruß.et: From Middle High German ruoȥ, rūȥ, from Old High German ruoȥ, hruoȥ, from Proto-Germanic *hrōtaz (“soot”), from Proto-Indo-European *kreH(u)d-.

s: armament (the act of acquiring or producing weapons)

Russenmagazin.et: From Russen + Magazin, the second element possibly influenced by Russian магазин (magazin, “store”).

russländisch.et: Russland + -isch, (neological translation of the Russian term российский (rossijskij))

s: a municipality of Upper Austria, Austria
a municipality of Lower Austria, Austria
1912, Martin Luther, Lutherbibel von 1912, Mark 15:42 (with KJV translation)
And now when the even was come, because it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath,
Rüsttag.et: From rüsten + Tag. . First attested as " der ruſt tag" in the Luther Bible as a translation of Ancient Greek παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ).

s: know-how, skills needed for a task
a field of expertise needed for a task
sunset; (by extension) the end of a time period; chiefly in zur Rüste gehen
Rüste.et: Borrowed from Middle Low German rüste. Cognate with Dutch rust. Ablaut variant of German Rast, English rest.

s: synonym of Rüstzeit (“retreat for religious devotion”)
Rüste.et: From the verb rüsten (“to prepare, equip, arm”). Not related to the "rest" sense of Etymology 1.

s: Von 1950–1989 war es nicht erlaubt, sich als Rusine oder Ruthene zu bezeichnen; nur Ukrainer durfte man sich nennen.
From 1950 till 1989 it was not allowed to call oneself a Rusyn or Ruthenian; only Ukrainian was allowed.
Rusine.et: Borrowed from Carpathian Rusyn руси́н (rusýn), from Old East Slavic русинъ (rusinŭ), a derivative of Русь (Rusĭ, “Rus”).

Gegen Ende der 90er-Jahre bin ich immer die einzige Ausländerin in meiner Schulklasse gewesen. Bis plötzlich „die Russen“ kamen. Sie waren natürlich nicht alle „Russen“, sondern vor allem Russlanddeutsche.

Rüster.et: From Middle High German rust, with the same suffix as in Heister, Holunder, Wacholder, etc.

s: Rüsselsheim (a town in southern Hesse, Germany)
Russian bread, especially kinds containing potato flour
Wir rückten da hinein, machten mit russischem Pulver Feuer an und fanden auch etwas Russenbrot, das, angeröstet, zu Kakao ganz gut schmeckt.
We went in, made fire with Russian powder and also found some Russian bread, which, when roasted, tastes all right with cocoa.
a kind of highly substandard bread substitute that was fed to Soviet prisoners of war

Die Versuche über ein besonders herzustellendes Russenbrot haben ergeben, daß die günstigste Mischung sich aus 50% Roggenschrot, 20% Zuckerrübenschnitzel, 20% Zellmehl und 10% Strohmehl oder Laub ergibt.

The experiments for a specially produced bread for Russians have shown that the most convenient mixture is 50% coarse rye meal, 20% chopped sugar beets, 20% ground cellulose and 10% ground straw or leaves.
someone who holds pro-Russian views (according to some sources, especially used within right-wing circles)
Vor allem bei jüngeren Rechten sorgt dieser Kurs für Kritik und Häme. Die rechten Russlandfreunde bezeichnen sie als „Boomer“ oder „Russenstusser“.
Als „Russenstusser“ und „Westextremisten“, als „Feindzeugen“ und Feiglinge beschimpfen sich AfD-Politiker und ihr Vorfeld in den sozialen Medien.

Rüssler.et: By surface analysis, Rüssel (“trunk, snout”) + -er (“-er”). Often a shortening of Rüsselkäfer.

Russisch Roulette.et: Optionally undeclined neuter adjective as in fließend Wasser, trocken Brot, etc. Optionally capitalized because it is an idiomatic term.
